rationale: Video polysomnography and clinical histories characterize NREM parasomnia behaviors across Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia and multiple system atrophy. The measured events are behaviors arising in sleep. The cohort does not compare food exposures or waking visual episodes.

The transdiagnostic structural imaging review maps findings from visual hallucination groups across several disorders. It describes occipital and parietal associations. The included contrasts are imaging and diagnosis comparisons without a dried fig exposure.

SNCA duplication case histories, genetic results and a literature comparison describe motor and nonmotor presentations. Some duplication carriers had hallucinations, along with sleep and cognitive symptoms. The clinical feature is reported with genetic disease and does not measure a culinary effect.

The secondary comparison selected 16 dementia with Lewy bodies participants and 19 controls with both imaging and stimulation measurements. Average early visual responses to checkerboards and resting perfusion were similar, while the relationship between stimulation threshold and visual response differed. The authors cite the earlier stimulation dataset. No oral fig comparison was made.

Structural and functional imaging assess theory of mind tasks and social cognition in Parkinson disease. The clinical selection and laboratory tasks do not quantify changes in waking visual hallucinations after a food exposure.

The clinical review examines Parkinson visual function from acuity and eye movements to perceptions and hallucinations. It discusses overlapping diagnoses and medication context. None of these narrative observations compares dried fig intake with a Parkinson hallucination endpoint.

Postmortem dopaminergic neurons were compared for respiratory-chain defects and mitochondrial DNA. The patient table includes visual and multimodal hallucinations in some clinical histories. It supplies no prospective episode counts or dietary comparisons.

The completed AJNR review organizes causes of visual hallucinations by clinical presentation and characteristic imaging. Parkinson and Lewy body disease are part of a broader clinical differential. It summarizes imaging across conditions and does not present a fig study.

The Parkinson resting-state imaging study stratifies participants by depression and measures brain-network topology in different frequency bands. The frequencies refer to imaging signals. This is outside the frozen culinary exposure and clinical episode comparison.

A retrospective matched dementia comparison includes 125 Parkinson dementia, 250 dementia with Lewy bodies and 500 Alzheimer dementia cases. The past-month caregiver inventory uses a general hallucination item. Participant-level symptom comparisons across diagnoses do not supply a visual-only food effect.

The clinical cohort follows dopamine agonist discontinuation and tabulates visual hallucinations in individual drug-related histories. The comparison concerns medication withdrawal. It does not identify dried fig intake or compare episode rates after meals.

The synthesis evaluates risk factors for later Parkinson dementia and treats a history of hallucinations as a predictor. The pooled association concerns future dementia and heterogeneous clinical observations, with no dried fig comparison.

The review discusses distinct Parkinson visual measures, including acuity, visuoperceptual changes, illusions and formed visual hallucinations. Its clinical prevalence, genetic and pathophysiological summaries do not evaluate a dietary exposure.

This complete AJNR correspondence comments on the separate imaging review PMID26744445 and emphasizes molecular imaging in the visual hallucination differential. It supplies interpretive context without a new patient sample or fig comparison.

Postmortem receptor binding was compared with prior symptoms in Alzheimer and Lewy body dementia. The authors report a stronger psychotic-symptom association for delusions. The visual-specific group comparisons did not reach statistical significance. There is no dried fig exposure or episode rate.

The randomized Parkinson study compares a cognitive rehabilitation program with a control condition and follows imaging activation, connectivity and cognition. It does not test a dried fig exposure or visual hallucination frequency.

The memory clinic series relates pulvinar visibility across MRI sequences to the presence of prior visual hallucinations in people with dementia. Time after a food exposure and Parkinson-specific episode counts were not measured.

This systems-biology synthesis compiles copy-number variants, genes and networks associated with Parkinson presentations. The comparisons concern genetic susceptibility and mechanisms. It does not provide a culinary exposure group or episode follow-up.

The Parkinson clinical and genetic study observes greater prevalence of visual hallucinations in mutation carriers than noncarriers (47% versus 22%) in the cited comparison. Time-to-event models estimate first progression to a feature. Neither measure isolates food intake or episode frequency.

The functional imaging comparison uses an attentional task in Lewy body dementia, Alzheimer dementia and controls. The hallucination subscale characterizes the groups. Task-linked network connectivity is the primary comparison, without a fig exposure.

A cohort of 298 Parkinson patients investigates genetic associations with developing dementia and a dopaminergic imaging subset. Clinical histories and frontostriatal outcomes do not supply a dried fig intervention or visual episode-rate estimate.

The original measures cerebrospinal fluid protein biomarkers across Lewy body disorders and Alzheimer dementia. Fatty acid binding protein is a laboratory biomarker here. The diagnostic classification comparison does not measure food consumption or visual symptom frequency.

The open-label amantadine extension records visual hallucinations in 43 participants (19.3%). These are participants with a reported adverse event during follow-up, with no concurrent food comparison. Prior trial exposure and age are relevant to interpretation.

The review maps genetic candidates associated with levodopa response and adverse events, including several hallucination studies. The intervention and dependency are clinical pharmacology. It provides no independent evidence of a dried fig effect.

The nonpharmacologic Lewy body dementia review includes psychological approaches addressing distress from visual hallucinations. The separate dietary fluid and postural trial addresses swallowing and aspiration. The distinct members provide no joint fig and visual outcome.

The MRI paper compares white and gray matter changes across Parkinson cognitive groups. Its clinical and neuropsychological comparisons concern cognition and volume. It has no dried fig exposure or longitudinal visual episode measure.

The Parkinson comparison measures reading speed and eye movements against age-matched controls. Visual hallucinations are among the symptoms in the clinical background. Reading performance is a separate endpoint.

The original diagnostic comparison assesses detection of disease-associated protein in brain and cerebrospinal fluid samples. The reported results concern assay discrimination. There is no culinary exposure or measured visual episode response.

The case-series and specialist-service records estimate clinical prevalence of dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson dementia. The visual feature contributes to diagnosis. The study estimates diagnosed patient proportions without dietary data.

The postmortem pulvinar comparison reports differences in transcripts and selected synaptic proteins in dementia with Lewy bodies. Clinical visual hallucinations frame the rationale. Tissue findings cannot supply the exposure or episode rate in the frozen claim.

The EEG groups compare slowing and frequency variability among Lewy body dementia, Alzheimer disease and controls. The analyses address fluctuating attention and arousal, with visual hallucinations discussed separately. There is no dietary contrast.

The panel reviews whether FDG-PET adds diagnostic utility in Parkinson and atypical parkinsonism with dementia. Only a small subset of the examined evidence supplies the critical diagnostic outcomes. The questions do not evaluate food or visual episode changes.

The retinal OCT study compares outer retinal structures in Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease and controls. It provides a structural vision measure, without repeated hallucination counts tied to fig intake.

A Parkinson imaging meta-analysis and independent resting-state validation address putamen activity. The cohorts and validation endpoints concern imaging under clinical conditions without a food exposure or hallucination count.

The postmortem study compares lysosomal enzyme activities in GBA-related and sporadic disorders. Cases were grouped by diagnosis and genotype, with limited symptom discrimination. It does not connect any dietary exposure to visual experiences.

The retrospective dementia cohorts compare relative survival by Lewy body or Parkinson dementia diagnosis. Hallucinations describe the syndrome. The tracked endpoint is survival without a detailed fig exposure or recurrent visual episode outcome.

The genetics review synthesizes loci, candidate pathways and disease classification for Lewy body dementia. Hallucinations are a clinical feature across syndromes discussed. The review has no food-exposed cohort or relevant efficacy outcome.

This neuroimaging review considers markers that may predict Parkinson dementia and discusses visuospatial and hallucination group findings. The research questions concern diagnostic and prognostic imaging rather than eating dried figs.

This diagnostic biomarker review covers prodromal symptoms, imaging, peripheral pathology and microbiota hypotheses. The gastrointestinal context is distinct from any measured fig exposure and provides no visual episode outcome.

The retrospective very mild dementia series reports visual hallucinations in 31.6% of dementia with Lewy bodies, 11.4% of Parkinson dementia and 4.0% of Alzheimer dementia participants. These are proportions by diagnosis. Dried fig exposure and rates of episodes per patient were not measured.

The cerebrospinal fluid study compares biomarker species by diagnosed cohort. The findings assess biomarkers and group discrimination. Neither a test food nor a visual frequency outcome enters the comparison.

The systematic review pools auditory and visual prevalence separately. Its visual prevalence estimate is 28.2% in Parkinson and 61.8% in dementia with Lewy bodies, with wide intervals and variation by ascertainment. The outcome is proportion of patients, with no exposure-stratified dried fig rate.

The Bulgarian genetic dementia cohort investigates repeat expansions and presents clinical cases. A case's increased food consumption and the broader comparison of sweet food preferences are behavioral features. No fig is specified and food was not assigned or linked to visual episode frequency.

The systematic review summarizes deep-brain stimulation in monogenic Parkinson disease, pooling case and cohort treatment reports. The intervention is surgical and not a dietary exposure. It does not measure fig-associated visual episodes.

Whole-exome and copy-number analyses in familial and sporadic Parkinson cases identify genetic candidates. The endpoint is variant identification. Visual or other symptoms in disease framing provide no evidence of an oral fig effect.

The postmortem Parkinson study associates hippocampal CA2 pathology with cholinergic degeneration and cognitive decline. Its tissue and diagnostic outcomes do not track the ingredient, preparation or visual episode frequency.

The cerebrospinal fluid study compares glial markers in Alzheimer and Lewy body dementia and early disease. Visual hallucinations contribute to clinical selection. The analysis concerns disease biomarkers, without dried fig exposure or episode timing.

The autopsy and longitudinal cognition report compares Alzheimer disease with additional clinically diagnosed or undiagnosed Lewy body pathology. Clinical records report the presence of hallucinations in some groups. Cognitive trajectories and proportions with symptoms do not estimate dietary response.

The Parkinson visual psychophysics experiment measures contextual modulation of contrast or related visual judgment tasks. Visual hallucinations appear in the broader clinical discussion. The applied visual stimuli are separate from the food exposure and spontaneous symptom.

The scoping review codes UK older adults' home-care needs. Chopping food appears as an example of functional limitation. It does not provide an ingredient comparison or a Parkinson visual hallucination outcome.

The clinical history summarizes Parkinson research and care in China. A description of adaptive spoons relates to eating with tremor, with no food intervention or visual hallucination efficacy analysis.

The neuroimaging synthesis includes nine studies of Parkinson hallucination groups alongside separate dementia and cognitive analyses. Coordinate convergence and anatomical network projections address spatial localization. No underlying dried fig comparison or exposure-specific episode rate is reported.

The Parkinson MRI cohort relates nonmotor symptom-scale scores to thalamic volume. Sleep and gastrointestinal subscores contribute to the association. The gastrointestinal subscore is a separate symptom measure without an assigned fig exposure or a visual episode outcome.

Computational network modeling compares vulnerability and connectivity as explanations of neurodegenerative patterns. Model fit and regional pathology are the outcomes. The paper supplies no food assignment or visual hallucination outcome.

Of 111 Parkinson patients with usable sonography, 18 reported visual hallucinations. The authors use presence as a binary outcome to model association with substantia nigra echogenicity and covariates. It is not an episode count or dietary comparison.

The PET study replicates a Parkinson glucose metabolism pattern across three cohorts and discusses medication state. Glucose metabolism is a tracer-based imaging outcome here. It does not represent fig intake or a visual episode measurement.

A laboratory visual learning task compares 17 Lewy body participants with hallucinations, 20 without and 20 controls. Prior visual templates improved disambiguation more in the hallucinator group. The task measures an effect of prior information on perception, without oral fig or clinical episode rates.
